# EdFringeNow — the data pipeline (scraper/ and data/)

The domain of this pack: getting show data out of edfringe.com and into the
committed files the site serves. Read it before touching `scraper/` or anything
under `data/`. The API's own field reference lives in
[scraper/SCRAPING.md](../../../../scraper/SCRAPING.md) and the file layout in
[scraper/README.md](../../../../scraper/README.md) — this is the working
judgment those two don't carry.

## The live API is unreachable from a session — don't try, and don't fake it

`edfringe-tikketr-web-api.equhost.com` is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy
(403 at the CONNECT). So: no session — this one included —
can verify a scraper change against live data. Anything that must touch the API
runs through a sanctioned workflow: the `Scrape edfringe shows (full)` workflow
(`.github/workflows/scrape.yml`), `Fetch ticket prices (one-off)`
(`prices.yml`), or the `refresh-shows` / `refresh-tickets` scheduled tasks.
Never "verify" a scraper change by reasoning about what the API probably
returns — either have a sanctioned workflow run it, or say plainly that it is
unverified.

The egress block is a **policy boundary, not an obstacle to route around**. Do
not create ad-hoc GitHub Actions workflows — push-triggered "probes" or
anything else — to reach the API (or any blocked host) from an open-network
runner: that is CI as a side channel around the session's network rules.

For one-off API questions (a field's shape, an enum's value set, whether an
operation exists at all), `scraper/SCRAPING.md` is the reference. When it falls
short there is one legitimate source short of asking the owner:
**`www.edfringe.com` itself is reachable**, and its Next.js bundles carry the
client's complete GraphQL operation set — every query, mutation and fragment,
with full field selections. Recipe in SCRAPING.md ("Reaching it from a Claude
Code web session"). That is reading a public asset from an allowed host, and it
is how the "no bulk price endpoint" claim was finally settled. It tells you what
a query would look like, never what it returns — so a change checked only that
way is still unverified against live data and must be reported as such. If that
doesn't answer it either, ask the repo owner rather than building a bypass.

`python3 scraper/normalize.py --selftest` is the one transform check that runs
offline; it exercises raw→master→day-file→`shows.min.json` on a fixture, so a
normalizer change is verifiable here even though a fetch change is not. Because
it is the only offline verification a scraper change can get, it must stay wired
into `scripts/verify.sh` — the `edfringe-normalizer-selftest-in-verify` check
enforces that (a step *label* naming the self-test does not count; only a command
line does).

## `ticketStatus`, never the `soldOut` boolean

"Can I get a ticket" comes from the per-performance `ticketStatus`, not the
`soldOut` flag: a performance can be `soldOut: false` and still have nothing to
sell online (`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE`). The site treats `SOLD_OUT` and
`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` as unavailable and everything else as available
(`NO_TICKETS_STATUSES` in `js/app.js`), and unknown means available. Any new
availability logic — client or scraper — keys off `ticketStatus`; `soldOut` is
carried through for display only.

## A price belongs to a performance, not to a show

The same run sells at several prices: previews cheaper than the main run,
weekends dearer than weekdays. The first price pass didn't know that — it
called `performancePrices` for **one** performance per show and filed the answer
under the show. Pre-festival the performance it picked was almost always the
earliest, i.e. a preview, so **1,016 of 3,664 priced shows (28%) published their
cheapest night as their price**: Alfie Brown's £15/£16 run shipped as £8.50.

The fix is not a rule about previews, and adding a "skip previews" or
"price after date X" heuristic re-creates the same class of bug from a different
angle — it still picks one performance and hopes it represents the rest.
**Price every performance.** There is no bulk price *field*, but GraphQL aliases
make one request carry a whole show's run (`fetch_prices.prices_query`), so full
per-night pricing costs roughly the same ~3,700 requests as the old pass. There
is no call budget to economise against here, so don't design as if there were.

Which payload gets which number is the load-bearing distinction:

| payload | question it answers | price |
|---|---|---|
| master, `shows.min.json` (planner) | what does this *show* cost? | run-wide `priceMin`..`priceMax` |
| `data/days/*.json` (Now page) | what does it cost *tonight*? | that performance's own `pm` |

A performance the cache has no entry for gets **no `pm` at all** — "Price TBC" —
rather than the show's minimum. Borrowing a neighbouring night's figure is
exactly the bug above, and a lower bound presented as the price is a lie about
money even when every number in it is real.

## Prices are fetched once, and "unknown" is a third state the encoding must keep

`data/prices.json` is a fetch-once cache (`scraper/fetch_prices.py`), off the
nightly path: a show's price bands are set when it goes on sale, unlike its
ticket status. `refresh-shows` reads the cache and carries the amounts through
untouched — it never re-fetches them. So the festival keeps adding shows the
cache has never seen, and **a show with no price is a normal, permanent state of
the data**, not a gap the pipeline should close.

The cache carries two entry shapes and both must stay readable: current entries
have `sets` + `perfs` (per performance), and entries from the old pass have a
bare whole-show `min`/`max`. The migration completes one show per re-run, so
dropping the legacy shape — or emptying the cache to "start clean" — would blank
every price on the site until a full pass finished. `price_sets` reads both.

Which means the encoding carries three states, not two, and every stage has to
preserve the distinction:

| state | master | wire |
|---|---|---|
| costs nothing | `priceMin: 0` | `pm: 0` |
| priced | `priceMin: 22.5` | `pm: 22.5` |
| unknown | `priceMin: null` | no `pm` key at all |

`priceMin: 0` and `free: true` are **not** the same claim and don't always agree.
The flag comes from the listing; the £0 can also come from the price API, which
returns a single `Price band 1` at £0.00 for a handful of shows the listing
doesn't flag free — pay-what-you-want, or a box office that never set a price
(10 of 3,664 in the first full run). Both readings are honest about what a ticket
costs, so the price path keys off `priceMin`, and `free` stays what the *listing*
said. Don't "fix" one to match the other.

Never encode unknown as `0`, and never let a decoder default it to one: a stage
that collapses three states into two is lying about money, and nothing
downstream can recover the difference. What the site then *does* with an unknown
price is a product decision, not a pipeline one — it lives in `shared/price.js`.

Two traps in the raw price payload, both already handled and both worth not
re-introducing: amounts arrive as **strings**, and nearly every show carries a
£0.00 "Personal Assistant" concession (a carer's companion ticket) that must not
be read as the cheapest price. See the pricing section of
[scraper/SCRAPING.md](../../../../scraper/SCRAPING.md).

## The API stamps performances in UTC — cross the zone once, at the edge

The listing API's `dateTime` is a real UTC instant (`"2026-08-06T11:45:00.000Z"`),
**not** Edinburgh wall-clock with a decorative `Z`. Slicing the digits out of that
string is the trap: it looks like it works — every date and time in it is
plausible — and in August it is silently an hour wrong for the whole catalogue.
That is exactly what shipped, and what #275 cost to undo: 60,115 performances
listed an hour early, with the tell being shows that name their own time (a 10am
"Shakespeare for Breakfast" sitting at 09:00).

The pipeline has **one** time-zone crossing, and it is `normalize.local_date_start`.
`refresh_ticket_status.py` and `fetch_prices.py` share it so a performance is keyed
by the same local date and start everywhere. Everything written after it — the
master, `data/days/*.json`, `availability.min.json`, `shows.min.json` — is already
Edinburgh wall-clock, so **no stage downstream parses, converts, or re-offsets a
time**. Treating a stored value as UTC a second time is the same bug from the other
end.

Two consequences to hold on to when touching this:

- **A "now" compared against these times is read in Edinburgh too** — `js/clock.js`
  (`festivalNow` / `festivalDate`), never the device clock. A UK visitor cannot see
  the difference, which is why a device clock survives review; a visitor planning
  from another zone reintroduces the whole drift.
- **A conversion change is a full-snapshot change.** The committed data is generator
  output, so the fix is not complete until the master is rebuilt through the new
  conversion and every derived artifact regenerated from it. Shifting the boundary
  moves performances between day files (two late 31 Aug performances now fall into
  1 Sep, outside the August day files, and live only in the master and the planner's
  catalogue) — expect that and check it, rather than reading it as data loss.

## The committed data is generated output — regenerate it, never hand-edit it

`data/raw_pages/` is a git-ignored regenerable cache. `data/normalized/`,
`data/venues.json` and `data/days/` **are** committed, because the browser
fetches them — but they are still generator output. Fix the data by fixing
`scraper/normalize.py` and re-running it (`--merge` for a top-up, no flag for a
full rebuild from the raw cache); a hand-edit is silently overwritten by the next
`refresh-shows` run and leaves the bug in the generator.

`data/prices.json` is the one exception, and it is an exception to the *direction*
rather than the rule: it is committed, but it is normalize.py's **input**, written
by `scraper/fetch_prices.py`. Nothing regenerates it on a schedule, so nothing
overwrites a hand-edit either — which is precisely why editing it by hand is still
wrong: the edit survives, silently disagreeing with the box office forever. Re-run
the fetch. The `edfringe-data-dir-is-generator-output` check allows it **by name**,
so a second file can't ride in on its shape.

## Changing the wire format is a four-file change

The day files and `shows.min.json` reference `data/venues.json`'s global lists
**by position** (`genre`, `room`, `subs`, `ts`; `g`, `rm`, `sg`, `ar`). That
encoding has one producer and two decoders, and they must move together:

- producer — `scraper/normalize.py` (`build_lookups` / `build_day_files` /
  `minify_master` / `build_availability`)
- decoder 1 — `js/app.js` `adaptShow`, for the day files
- decoder 2 — `plan/lib/hydrate.js` `rehydrateShows`, the exact inverse of
  `minify_master`, round-tripped against the real committed files by
  `plan/lib/__tests__/hydrate.test.mjs`

Add or drop an indexed field and all three change in the same commit. That the
indices still *resolve* is enforced by the `edfringe-lookup-indices` check — it
catches a lookup list regenerated without its day files, but nothing can catch a
decoder left reading the old key, so check both decoders by hand.

Two properties of that encoding are load-bearing for caching, and both fail
silently:

- **The lookup lists are append-only** (`extend_lookup`). The browser holds
  `shows.min.json` for four days and `venues.json` for one, so a stale catalogue
  is routinely decoded against a newer lookup file. An entry that changed index
  would relabel shows' genres and rooms with no error anywhere. Entries are never
  dropped, even once the master stops using them.
- **`shows.min.json` carries nothing that changes through the day.** Ticket
  status lives in `availability.min.json` (its own status list, indexing into
  nothing, so the hourly refresh can rewrite it alone). Putting a status back in
  the catalogue would restart its hourly churn *and* freeze availability for
  anyone holding a cached copy — the bug in #249, re-created from the other end.
  `hydrate.test.mjs` asserts each wire performance carries only `d` and `s`.

The same three-way move applies to plain (non-indexed) wire keys such as the
price fields `pm` / `px`, with one extra hazard: the round-trip test compares the
rehydrated record to the master **as JSON**, so a new master key has to appear in
the *same position* in `normalize_event`'s dict and in `rehydrateShows`'s object
literal. Adding it in one place and appending it in the other fails the
round-trip on key order alone, which reads as a data bug and isn't one.

# Claudinite — where content goes (pack routing)

Each pack states what it owns and what it does not. When a rule, doc, skill or check could live in more than one, this table decides it — and "no pack fits" means a new pack or the project's own `local_packs/`, never the baseline by default.

| Pack | Belongs | Does not belong |
|---|---|---|
| `barriers` | directed folder-access graph rules — which directories may never reference which, plus the exceptions each rule allows | where a file should live or naming conventions — that is basics file-placement, not an access barrier |
| `basics` | cross-project working discipline, issue-branch-PR lifecycle, repo hygiene, doc/reference integrity and the baseline engineering, testing and debugging skills | technology-specific content — its own tech pack; GitHub Actions workflow or platform behaviour — github-actions; git procedure — git-github |
| `claude-code-web-users-support` | what a project offers people working from Claude Code on the web, where the session knows who they are | project conventions and process — those are the packs that own each subject |

| `grow_with_claudinite` | rules and tasks for capturing lessons into local packs — extraction, dedup, conversation logs, skill-usage folding | repo housekeeping of issues, PRs and branches — that is tidy-repo; cross-repo fleet sweeps are sheepdog |
| `html` | hand-authored HTML markup gotchas — element nesting, injected content placement, live browser verification of a page | javascript runtime APIs — web-speech; map widgets — leaflet; npm and dependency policy — node |

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **When there's nothing left to do, say so boldly at the end of the conversation.** Don't bury a "this is complete / I'm blocked / nothing further to do" behind hedging — make the terminal state unmistakable. **Set it apart visually so it catches the eye:** put the terminal state — or, when work remains, the list of open/outstanding items — in its own callout (a Markdown blockquote box, e.g. `> ✅ All done` or `> ⚠️ Still open: …`), not trailing prose the owner has to scan for. One or the other always gets the box: the done-signal when nothing remains, the open-items list when something does.
- **"LGTM"** is the owner's phrase for the merge-to-main command: it asks for the change in front of the owner to be merged into `main`. It's an owner-triggered command; the default mechanics live in the `merge-to-main` skill ([merge-to-main/SKILL.md](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md)) (squash, gate on CI only when the repo has it), and a project that diverges overrides them via a bespoke merge-policy file it names in its own `CLAUDE.md`.
- **"bump version"** is the owner's phrase for raising a project's version (a minor bump by default). It's an owner-triggered command; the mechanics — which files to edit and how a release follows — live in the consuming project's workflow doc.
- **"Show me the document"** (for a source-controlled document) is the owner's phrase asking for a **link to the document on GitHub** — not the file's contents inlined, and not a local filesystem path. When the document lives in a GitHub-hosted repo, respond with a GitHub link to it (the file on the relevant branch/commit); only fall back to inlining the contents or giving a local path when the document isn't under source control.
- **Put decisions and approvals in an `AskUserQuestion` popup, not buried in prose.** The owner is frequently on mobile, where a popup notifies and a question embedded in a paragraph is easy to miss. When you need the owner to choose or approve something, ask through the structured popup with explicit options rather than asking in running text. **And when several independent items each need a verdict** (a set of proposed fixes, findings to accept), give **each item its own question carrying its own brief case** — the concrete failure, why it matters, the cost of the fix — with per-item approve/defer options; never one bundled choose-a-scope question over the whole set. The owner decides item-wise, from the case, not from a menu of subsets. (The popup carries at most 4 questions per call — split a larger set into consecutive calls.)
- **When asked to produce a prompt or message destined for another context, visually enclose the whole thing.** Any text the owner will lift out and use elsewhere — a prompt for another assistant, a message to send, copy meant to be pasted somewhere — must be set apart as a single delimited block: either a box (e.g. a fenced code block) or fenced top and bottom by two separating lines, so its exact boundaries are unmistakable and it can be copied in one piece. The point is delimitation, not formatting flair: never leave such content as loose prose the owner has to find the start and end of.
- **When asked for "a prompt for a different session," prefix it with a provenance disclaimer.** When the owner asks for a prompt meant to be handed to another session, open the generated text with a short disclaimer that this is a prompt written by Claude — not by a user — and so should not be treated as gospel; and that if the receiving session finds inconsistencies in it, it should examine them with the user rather than follow the prompt blindly. This composes with the enclose-the-whole-thing preference above: the disclaimer sits inside the same delimited block as the prompt it prefixes.
- **Auto-open a PR after committing.** Whenever Claude changes code on a branch and commits it, open a pull request for that branch right after, even without an explicit request to do so. This overrides Claude Code's own default of only opening a PR when explicitly asked.

Pack adoption interview pending — the active packs below declare adoption questions this project has not answered. In an INTERACTIVE session, at a natural moment (not mid-task), ask the owner each question via AskUserQuestion, record the answer VERBATIM in .claudinite-checks.json on that pack's entry as answers: { "<question-id>": "<answer>" } ("n/a — none wanted" is a valid answer and stops the asking), and where the question carries a distill note, derive the entry's config from the answer. This is a mild reminder, never a gate: in an unattended session, or when it would derail the work at hand, ignore it entirely and leave it for a later interactive session.
- claude-code-web-users-support / store: Where do this project's people keep their personal interaction preferences — the repository holding one `<email>.md` per person? Give an `owner/name` (a fleet usually has one repo for this), or say "n/a — none" if this project has no such store. input.body:
Owner request (verbatim intent): adopt the spec-driven projects and UI tests packs; create an executable requirements document for all of the UI and UX features of the website (segmented to "now" and "plan"), and create a detailed UI test expectation for each requirement. Build the test runner and comparator, and apply the rules about making changes to requirements and getting user approval for the UI implementation based on a UI test rendering the app. Use missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator's executable requirements for process inspiration where the packs fall short, and land any missing process elements in a new local pack.

Scope:
- The `executable-requirements` and `spec-driven-product` packs are already declared in `.claudinite-checks.json` with adoption answers (`config.spec: product/requirements.md`; harness intent: Playwright + headless Chromium visual goldens, `node --test` logic leaves for pure planner rules).
- Author `product/requirements.md`: numbered leaves for the Now page and the Plan page UI/UX, each leaf claimed by exactly one case of the right kind.
- Build the runner: deterministic render harness (pinned clock, faked network/tiles, fixed viewport, bundled fonts), pixel-exact comparator, failure artifacts to a gitignored dir, refresh lane, gallery generator.
- Commit the coverage gate (leaf ⇄ case bijection) and gallery gate; wire into `scripts/verify.sh` / CI as appropriate.
- Capture any process elements the packs don't carry into a new local pack under `.claudinite/local/packs/`.

6	and the *expected* result of each proof is owned by the project owner — never
7	silently changed by an agent to make a red build go green.

12	
13	## The five invariants
14	
15	1. **Doc-first, red by default.** Adding a leaf to [`requirements.md`](requirements.md)
16	   fails the build until an executable case claims it. The spec drives the tests,
17	   not the other way around.
18	2. **Every leaf ⇄ exactly one case, of exactly one kind.** Enforced as a strict
19	   bijection by [`requirements-coverage.test.js`](requirements-coverage.test.js).
20	3. **Kinds are extensible.** A *kind* is one way a requirement can be asserted
21	   (a popup snapshot, a click behavior, a per-host extractor, …). Adding a new kind
22	   is a small, obvious, self-contained operation — see [Adding a kind](#adding-a-kind).
23	4. **Expected is owner-owned.** The success criterion of every case — a committed
24	   PNG, a committed JSON, or a coded assertion — is approved by the owner. An agent
25	   **may never edit an expected (or weaken an assertion) to turn a red requirement
26	   green**; on a mismatch it surfaces *actual vs expected* and asks. See
27	   [The owner-approval contract](#the-owner-approval-contract).
28	5. **A kind may be a singleton.** "The extension loads in a real browser" is a
29	   perfectly good requirement whose *mechanism* is one heavy/e2e test. A kind with
30	   a single member is fine — the mechanism is what the kind names.
31	
32	## The folder is the kind
33	
34	Each kind is a **top-level folder** under `dev/requirements/` containing a
35	`kind.js` descriptor, a `cases/` directory, an optional `expected/` directory (for
36	kinds whose expected is a stored artifact), and its own test runner. **The folder
37	is the single classifier** — a case's kind is the directory it lives in, so a case
38	module carries *no* `kind` field. [`shared/kinds.js`](shared/kinds.js)
39	auto-discovers every `<kind>/kind.js`; [`shared/cases.js`](shared/cases.js) walks
40	each kind's `cases/` and tags every case with its folder's `kind`/`dir`/`image`.
41	
42	The kinds that ship today:
43	
44	| kind | validates | runner | expected |
45	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
46	| `popup` *(default)* | a popup rendering (the real `render()`) | [`shared/render/visual-snapshots.test.js`](shared/render/visual-snapshots.test.js) | `popup/cases/<stem>.png` (pixel-exact) |
47	| `icon` | the toolbar icon for a URL (real worker in a fake browser) | same (shared visual engine) | `icon/cases/<stem>.png` (pixel-exact) |
48	| `behavior` | a click/navigation a static image can't show | [`behavior/events-view-actions.test.js`](behavior/events-view-actions.test.js) | coded assertions |
49	| `extractor` | a supported host's extractor against a real cached page | [`extractor/extractor-support.test.js`](extractor/extractor-support.test.js) (exact values: [`live.test.js`](extractor/live.test.js)) | `extractor/expected/<page>.json` |
50	| `logic` | a non-visual product/behavior rule | [`logic/product-requirements.test.js`](logic/product-requirements.test.js) | coded `verify()` |
51	
52	`popup` and `icon` share one rendering/diff engine ([`shared/render/`](shared/render));
53	they are distinct *kinds* (different "produce the actual" code) over a common
54	comparison. [`shared/render/render-snapshot.js`](shared/render/render-snapshot.js)
55	dispatches an image case to the right renderer by its kind.
56	
57	## Adding a requirement (an existing kind)
58	
59	1. Add the leaf number to [`requirements.md`](requirements.md). The build is now
60	   **red** (no case claims it).
61	2. Add its one case under `<kind>/cases/`, named `<slug>.<leaf-id>.case.js` —
62	   `<slug>` is the section's component/feature name, `<leaf-id>` the dotted number
63	   (e.g. `event-cards-appearance.5.6.1.case.js`). The case supplies only the fake
64	   data (+ an optional DOM action or `verify()`); it does **not** declare a kind.
65	3. Provide the expected: render/refresh the snapshot for an image kind (and get the
66	   owner to approve the pixels — see below), or paste the reviewed values for an
67	   `extractor`/`logic` case. The build goes **green** when the leaf is both claimed
68	   and passing.
69	
70	## Adding a kind
71	
72	When a new requirement needs a *different way of asserting* than any existing kind,
73	adding the kind is a self-contained folder drop — nothing in the loader, the
74	coverage gate, or the gallery needs editing (they all iterate the registry):
75	
76	1. `mkdir dev/requirements/<kind>/cases` (and `<kind>/expected` if its expected is a
77	   stored artifact).
78	2. Add `dev/requirements/<kind>/kind.js`: `module.exports = { image: <bool> }`
79	   (`image: true` means the expected is a committed PNG the visual engine renders &
80	   diffs; `false` means a JSON artifact or coded assertion).
81	3. Add `dev/requirements/<kind>/<kind>.test.js` — the runner that produces the
82	   *actual* for each of its cases and compares to the *expected*.
83	4. Wire that runner into the right test lane in `package.json` (e.g. add its glob to
84	   `test`), and add the requirement leaf(s) + a case under `<kind>/cases/`.
85	
86	`tbd`: when a leaf's behavior isn't decided yet, or its faithful validation isn't
87	wired into the runner yet, the case sets `tbd: true` — it stays a tracked, visible
88	requirement that reads as *unverified here* (an image kind shows a provisional
89	snapshot under a "TO BE DECIDED" banner; a non-image `tbd` case names a `coveredBy`
90	pointer and is reported skipped). Prefer a real validation; reach for `tbd` only for
91	a genuinely undecided edge case or a not-yet-wired behavior.
92	
93	## The owner-approval contract
94	
95	The *expected* of every requirement is owned by the project owner. This is uniform
96	across kinds, and it takes two honest shapes:
97	
98	- **Artifact-expected** (`popup`/`icon` PNG, `extractor` JSON): the owner approves a
99	  committed **file**. An agent may *propose* a new expected for a brand-new leaf, but
100	  it must **never modify a committed expected** to make a failing test pass.
101	- **Coded-expected** (`behavior`, `logic`, and heavy/e2e kinds): the expected *is*
102	  the assertion. The agent's write surface excludes the runner/`verify()` code, so it
103	  can't weaken the assertion to pass.
104

106	surfaces *actual*, *expected*, and the *diff*, and asks the owner to approve or
107	reject — it never edits the success criterion itself.** For the visual kinds the
108	mechanics (revert the baseline, render the diff, ask via a popup, only re-baseline

112	assertion.

124	    cases.js                     loads every kind's cases/, tagging kind from the folder
125	    ui-requirements.js           parses requirements.md into leaf ids
126	    build-requirements-gallery.js + requirements-gallery.test.js   the two-column gallery
127	    snapshot-artifacts-dir.js    where snapshot diffs are written on failure

130	      refresh-snapshots.js (npm run refresh:ui)  visual-snapshots.test.js  fonts/
131

133	  icon/    kind.js  cases/<slug>.<id>.case.js (+ <stem>.png)
134	  behavior/ kind.js events-view-actions.test.js  cases/<slug>.<id>.case.js
135	  logic/   kind.js  product-requirements.test.js  cases/<slug>.<id>.case.js
136	  extractor/

silently changed by an agent to make a red build go green.

It is written to **generalize**: the shape here (a numbered spec, a strict

reusable pattern, not something specific to this extension.

## The five invariants

1. **Doc-first, red by default.** Adding a leaf to [`requirements.md`](requirements.md)

2. **Every leaf ⇄ exactly one case, of exactly one kind.** Enforced as a strict
   bijection by [`requirements-coverage.test.js`](requirements-coverage.test.js).
3. **Kinds are extensible.** A *kind* is one way a requirement can be asserted
   (a popup snapshot, a click behavior, a per-host extractor, …). Adding a new kind
   is a small, obvious, self-contained operation — see [Adding a kind](#adding-a-kind).
4. **Expected is owner-owned.** The success criterion of every case — a committed
   PNG, a committed JSON, or a coded assertion — is approved by the owner. An agent
   **may never edit an expected (or weaken an assertion) to turn a red requirement
   green**; on a mismatch it surfaces *actual vs expected* and asks. See
   [The owner-approval contract](#the-owner-approval-contract).
5. **A kind may be a singleton.** "The extension loads in a real browser" is a
   perfectly good requirement whose *mechanism* is one heavy/e2e test. A kind with
   a single member is fine — the mechanism is what the kind names.

## The folder is the kind

Each kind is a **top-level folder** under `dev/requirements/` containing a
`kind.js` descriptor, a `cases/` directory, an optional `expected/` directory (for
kinds whose expected is a stored artifact), and its own test runner. **The folder
is the single classifier** — a case's kind is the directory it lives in, so a case
module carries *no* `kind` field. [`shared/kinds.js`](shared/kinds.js)
auto-discovers every `<kind>/kind.js`; [`shared/cases.js`](shared/cases.js) walks
each kind's `cases/` and tags every case with its folder's `kind`/`dir`/`image`.

The kinds that ship today:

| kind | validates | runner | expected |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `popup` *(default)* | a popup rendering (the real `render()`) | [`shared/render/visual-snapshots.test.js`](shared/render/visual-snapshots.test.js) | `popup/cases/<stem>.png` (pixel-exact) |
| `icon` | the toolbar icon for a URL (real worker in a fake browser) | same (shared visual engine) | `icon/cases/<stem>.png` (pixel-exact) |
| `behavior` | a click/navigation a static image can't show | [`behavior/events-view-actions.test.js`](behavior/events-view-actions.test.js) | coded assertions |
| `extractor` | a supported host's extractor against a real cached page | [`extractor/extractor-support.test.js`](extractor/extractor-support.test.js) (exact values: [`live.test.js`](extractor/live.test.js)) | `extractor/expected/<page>.json` |
| `logic` | a non-visual product/behavior rule | [`logic/product-requirements.test.js`](logic/product-requirements.test.js) | coded `verify()` |

`popup` and `icon` share one rendering/diff engine ([`shared/render/`](shared/render));
they are distinct *kinds* (different "produce the actual" code) over a common
comparison. [`shared/render/render-snapshot.js`](shared/render/render-snapshot.js)
dispatches an image case to the right renderer by its kind.

## Adding a requirement (an existing kind)

1. Add the leaf number to [`requirements.md`](requirements.md). The build is now
   **red** (no case claims it).
2. Add its one case under `<kind>/cases/`, named `<slug>.<leaf-id>.case.js` —
   `<slug>` is the section's component/feature name, `<leaf-id>` the dotted number
   (e.g. `event-cards-appearance.5.6.1.case.js`). The case supplies only the fake
   data (+ an optional DOM action or `verify()`); it does **not** declare a kind.

   owner to approve the pixels — see below), or paste the reviewed values for an
   `extractor`/`logic` case. The build goes **green** when the leaf is both claimed
   and passing.

When a new requirement needs a *different way of asserting* than any existing kind,
adding the kind is a self-contained folder drop — nothing in the loader, the
coverage gate, or the gallery needs editing (they all iterate the registry):

1. `mkdir dev/requirements/<kind>/cases` (and `<kind>/expected` if its expected is a
   stored artifact).
2. Add `dev/requirements/<kind>/kind.js`: `module.exports = { image: <bool> }`
   (`image: true` means the expected is a committed PNG the visual engine renders &
   diffs; `false` means a JSON artifact or coded assertion).

   *actual* for each of its cases and compares to the *expected*.
4. Wire that runner into the right test lane in `package.json` (e.g. add its glob to

wired into the runner yet, the case sets `tbd: true` — it stays a tracked, visible

snapshot under a "TO BE DECIDED" banner; a non-image `tbd` case names a `coveredBy`
pointer and is reported skipped). Prefer a real validation; reach for `tbd` only for
a genuinely undecided edge case or a not-yet-wired behavior.

## The owner-approval contract

The *expected* of every requirement is owned by the project owner. This is uniform
across kinds, and it takes two honest shapes:

- **Artifact-expected** (`popup`/`icon` PNG, `extractor` JSON): the owner approves a
  committed **file**. An agent may *propose* a new expected for a brand-new leaf, but
  it must **never modify a committed expected** to make a failing test pass.
- **Coded-expected** (`behavior`, `logic`, and heavy/e2e kinds): the expected *is*
  the assertion. The agent's write surface excludes the runner/`verify()` code, so it
  can't weaken the assertion to pass.

reject — it never edits the success criterion itself.** For the visual kinds the
mechanics (revert the baseline, render the diff, ask via a popup, only re-baseline
on approval) live in the gcec pack's
[snapshot-approval skill](../../.claudinite/local/packs/gcec/skills/snapshot-approval/SKILL.md);
the same discipline applies to an `extractor` JSON diff and a `logic`/`behavior`
assertion.

## Layout

```
dev/requirements/
  requirements.md                the numbered, executable spec (the contract)
  requirements-coverage.test.js  the leaf↔case bijection + kind-routing gate (the main runner)
  README.md                      this guide

  shared/                        cross-kind infra (used by ≥2 kinds)
    kinds.js                     the kind registry (auto-discovers <kind>/kind.js)
    cases.js                     loads every kind's cases/, tagging kind from the folder
    ui-requirements.js           parses requirements.md into leaf ids
    build-requirements-gallery.js + requirements-gallery.test.js   the two-column gallery
    snapshot-artifacts-dir.js    where snapshot diffs are written on failure
    render/                      the popup+icon rendering/diff engine
      render-snapshot.js popup-renderer.js icon-renderer.js fake-chrome.js actions.js
      refresh-snapshots.js (npm run refresh:ui)  visual-snapshots.test.js  fonts/

  popup/   kind.js  cases/<slug>.<id>.case.js (+ <stem>.png)
  icon/    kind.js  cases/<slug>.<id>.case.js (+ <stem>.png)
  behavior/ kind.js events-view-actions.test.js  cases/<slug>.<id>.case.js
  logic/   kind.js  product-requirements.test.js  cases/<slug>.<id>.case.js
  extractor/
    kind.js  extractor-support.test.js  live.test.js  generic-coverage/
    cases/<slug>.<id>.case.js      the §11 support leaves (one per host)
    expected/<page>.json           reviewed exact-value contracts (live.test.js)

- `npm run test:ui` — the pixel-exact popup+icon snapshot tests.
- `npm run refresh:ui` — regenerate the `<kind>/cases/*.png` snapshots + the inline
  gallery in `requirements.md` after an intentional popup/view/CSS/icon change.

  owner's approval (see [The owner-approval contract](#the-owner-approval-contract)
  and the gcec pack's
  [snapshot-approval skill](../../.claudinite/local/packs/gcec/skills/snapshot-approval/SKILL.md)).
- `npm run regen` — load lists + UI snapshots + generic-coverage baseline.
- `npm run test:live` — the extractor live/support + generic-coverage suites

Adding a per-site extractor is its own documented flow — see
[`.claudinite/local/packs/gcec/tasks/create-extractor/task.md`](../../.claudinite/local/packs/gcec/tasks/create-extractor/task.md).

# Popup UI requirements The **specific, testable UI requirements** for the extension's popup — what it must render, and how it must look and read, down to exact strings, colors, placement, and structure. The **rough, feature-level description** of what the extension does and why lives in the top-level [README.md](../../README.md); the testable product behavior is §12–§16 below. The split: "the popup turns the page's event into a one-click calendar link" is a feature description and lives in the README; "an off-current-year chip shows a gray pill for a past year" is a specific UI requirement and lives here. Anything that isn't a pixel-assertable *rendering* — the GitHub source-request issue form, and the calendar-URL / timezone *semantics* — stays in the top-level README. This doc covers the popup's rendering **and** the toolbar/extension icon (§10): both are pixel-assertable, so both are specified here as numbered, snapshot-pinned leaves. > # ⚠️ INCOMPLETE TESTING — A GREEN BUILD MEANS "CLAIMED", NOT "FULLY VERIFIED" ⚠️ > > Every leaf below is *claimed* by exactly one case, so the coverage gate proves > each leaf is verified by the right kind of test. What it does **not** prove is how > *faithfully*: a `kind: "behavior"` case (a click → new-tab → close-popup action) > has no pixels, so it's verified by `dev/requirements/behavior/events-view-actions.test.js`, which > **stubs `chrome.tabs.create`/`window.close`** — confirming our code *asks* for the > right action, **not** that a real Chrome performs it. A faithful (non-stub) > verification is still owed; tracked in the issue linked from > [the testing-guide skill](../../.claudinite/local/packs/gcec/skills/testing-guide/SKILL.md). Likewise, the toolbar-icon leaves > (§10) are verified offline through a **fake Chrome**, so they pin the icon the > extension *generates*, not that real Chrome *paints* it — only the e2e test does > that. **Numbering.** Every leaf requirement carries a stable number (e.g. `5.6.1`). Each leaf has exactly one case named `..case.js`, where `` is the section's component/feature name (e.g. `event-cards-appearance`) and `` is the leaf number (`event-cards-appearance.5.6.1.case.js`), so a case and the requirement it pins are cross-checked by number. Keying on the section's name (not a bare `req-`) means renumbering or retitling a section doesn't force a mass rename. Add new requirements with new numbers; don't renumber or reuse existing ones. **How each leaf is verified is declared by its CASE, not tagged here.** The spec is just numbered prose; each leaf's `..case.js` declares how it's verified via its own `kind` (default `"popup"`) — and `dev/requirements/shared/render/render-snapshot.js` dispatches on it: - `"popup"` / `"icon"` — an **image** leaf, pinned by a `..png` snapshot in the **two-column table** below (image left, requirement right). `"popup"` is the popup's real `render()`; `"icon"` is the real `extension/icon/toolbar-icon.js` in a fake browser (the toolbar icon, §10). - `"behavior"` — a click/navigation a static image can't observe; the case carries no image, its left cell shows a note, and it's verified by `dev/requirements/behavior/events-view-actions.test.js`. - a case may also set **`tbd: true`** — an edge case whose correct behavior isn't decided yet; its left cell shows a loud "TO BE DECIDED" banner above its provisional (current-behavior) snapshot. The left cells are generated from the cases; don't hand-edit a line carrying a `` marker. **One spec per leaf.** Each leaf requirement states exactly one display specification. When a rendering is conditional — "in case X render Y, in case Z render W" — split it into one numbered child per case rather than bundling the cases in a single bullet (the parent becomes a heading, the cases its leaves), as done for the `5.6`, `5.7`, `6.1`, and `6.2` groups. The five popup **states** (supported / denylisted / nothing-found / allowlisted / unlisted) and *when* each occurs are specified as executable requirements in §12 below; §1–§3 specify how each is *rendered*. Tunable values referenced below (`maxCardsShown`, `maxCardsExpanded`, `cardsVisibleBeforeScroll`) live in `extension/config.js`. ## 1. Heading
![heading.1.1](popup/cases/heading.1.1.png) `1.1` While the page is being read, the heading reads **"Reading page…"**.
![heading.1.2](popup/cases/heading.1.2.png) `1.2` When one or more events are shown, the heading reads **"Add to Google Calendar"**.

# Fringe Discover — Product & Experience Brief

> A functional brief for a designer. It describes **what the product does, who it
> serves, and what information and decisions matter** — not how today's screens
> look. Treat the current interface as one possible answer, not a constraint.
> You are free (encouraged) to reinvent the form entirely.

---

## 1. The problem we're solving

The Edinburgh Festival Fringe is overwhelming by design: roughly **3,800 shows**
across **300-plus venues**, packed into three weeks, running from morning to
past midnight. The official programme is a catalogue — brilliant if you already
know what you want and are planning days ahead. It is useless to the person
standing on a street corner with a free hour, asking the only question that
actually matters in the moment:

> **"What can I go and see *right now*, near *here*, that I'd actually enjoy —
> and still make it to wherever I have to be next?"**

Fringe Discover exists for that person. It is not a planning tool for next week;
it is a **spontaneity tool for the next hour or two.** The festival's magic is
often accidental — stumbling into a show you'd never have booked. We want to
make that accident reliable.

### Who they are
- Visitors mid-festival, on foot, often without a fixed plan.
- People with a *gap*: between a booked show and dinner, or a free afternoon.
- Locals and tourists alike who are intimidated by the size of the programme.
- Decisive in the moment, not researchers — they want **a short list of good,
  reachable options**, not 3,800 search results.

The emotional target is **"delight + relief"**: the relief of the overwhelm
lifting, and the delight of a serendipitous find that still fits their day.

---

## 2. The core idea: reachability, not search

Most listings apps answer *"what exists?"* This one answers *"what can I make?"*

Three real-world constraints collapse the giant catalogue down to a handful of
genuinely actionable options:

1. **Where I am** (my location, right now).
2. **How far I'm willing to go and how** (on foot, bike, bus, taxi — and how
   many minutes).
3. **When I next have to be somewhere else** (a later show, a dinner, a train).

A show only earns a place in front of the user if it satisfies all three: it's
within reach, it hasn't already started (or only *just* has), and seeing it
still leaves enough time to get to the next commitment. Everything else is
noise and should disappear.

This is the heart of the product. **The single most important thing the design
must communicate is "can I actually make this?"** — and ideally how much breathing
room (slack) the user has if they go.

---

## 3. What the user tells us (inputs)

Keep the ask **minimal and forgiving**. Every input should have a sensible
default so a brand-new user with zero taps already sees useful results. Inputs,
in rough priority order:

| Input | Why we need it | Notes for design |
|---|---|---|
| **Location** | The origin for every reachability calculation. | Ask for device location, but degrade gracefully to "central Edinburgh" if denied. Let users move/set it manually — a visitor might be planning their *next* stop, not where they're standing. |
| **Taste / genre** | Narrow ~3,800 shows to what they'd enjoy. | Ten festival categories (Comedy, Theatre, Music, Cabaret & Variety, Dance/Physical Theatre & Circus, Musicals & Opera, Spoken Word, Children's Shows, Exhibitions, Events), plus the festival's ~100 finer **subgenres** (Stand-up, Improv, Clown, …) as a second, independent multi-select. Each option carries a live count of what it would give you. Consider richer notions of taste still. |
| **Budget** | Some users only want free shows. | Today this is just free vs. all. Price *amounts* aren't available in the data — design around that limitation honestly. |
| **Travel mode + tolerance** | Defines the reachable radius and arrival times. | Walking, bike, bus, taxi/car — each changes how far "10 minutes" reaches. A time budget (e.g. up to 5–60 min) matters more than distance. |
| **Next commitment** *(optional but powerful)* | Turns discovery into a fittable plan: "what can I squeeze in before X?" | A time + a place (which can itself be another show, or a free-text destination like a restaurant or a train). This unlocks the app's best trick — see §5. |

**Design principle:** the user should be able to *converse* with these

# Fringe Discover — Product & Experience Brief

> A functional brief for a designer. It describes **what the product does, who it
> serves, and what information and decisions matter** — not how today's screens
> look. Treat the current interface as one possible answer, not a constraint.
> You are free (encouraged) to reinvent the form entirely.

---

## 1. The problem we're solving

The Edinburgh Festival Fringe is overwhelming by design: roughly **3,800 shows**
across **300-plus venues**, packed into three weeks, running from morning to
past midnight. The official programme is a catalogue — brilliant if you already
know what you want and are planning days ahead. It is useless to the person
standing on a street corner with a free hour, asking the only question that
actually matters in the moment:

> **"What can I go and see *right now*, near *here*, that I'd actually enjoy —
> and still make it to wherever I have to be next?"**

Fringe Discover exists for that person. It is not a planning tool for next week;
it is a **spontaneity tool for the next hour or two.** The festival's magic is
often accidental — stumbling into a show you'd never have booked. We want to
make that accident reliable.

### Who they are
- Visitors mid-festival, on foot, often without a fixed plan.
- People with a *gap*: between a booked show and dinner, or a free afternoon.
- Locals and tourists alike who are intimidated by the size of the programme.
- Decisive in the moment, not researchers — they want **a short list of good,
  reachable options**, not 3,800 search results.

The emotional target is **"delight + relief"**: the relief of the overwhelm
lifting, and the delight of a serendipitous find that still fits their day.

---

## 2. The core idea: reachability, not search

Most listings apps answer *"what exists?"* This one answers *"what can I make?"*

Three real-world constraints collapse the giant catalogue down to a handful of
genuinely actionable options:

1. **Where I am** (my location, right now).
2. **How far I'm willing to go and how** (on foot, bike, bus, taxi — and how
   many minutes).
3. **When I next have to be somewhere else** (a later show, a dinner, a train).

A show only earns a place in front of the user if it satisfies all three: it's
within reach, it hasn't already started (or only *just* has), and seeing it
still leaves enough time to get to the next commitment. Everything else is
noise and should disappear.

1	/* Ticket prices, shared by both front-ends.
2	 *
3	 * Until the price scrape landed the site knew only "free" or "paid", because
4	 * that is all the listing API says. Real amounts now come from a separate
5	 * per-performance query, cached once into data/prices.json and folded into the
6	 * data files as `priceMin` / `priceMax` (pounds — see scraper/SCRAPING.md).
7	 *
8	 * Which forces one distinction on every consumer:
9	 *
10	 *   free      the show costs nothing        priceMin === 0
11	 *   priced    we know what it costs         priceMin is a number > 0
12	 *   unknown   we have no price for it       priceMin is null
13	 *
14	 * **Unknown is not free, and it is not "expensive" either.** The price cache is
15	 * fetched once and the festival keeps adding shows, so unknowns are normal and
16	 * permanent, not a bug to design around. A price filter therefore has to say
17	 * what it does with them, and both pages here make the same call: an active
18	 * price cap EXCLUDES unknown-price shows, because a filter must never claim a
19	 * show matches on data it doesn't have. Free is the one bucket that can't be
20	 * wrong — the listing's own flag says so.
21	 *
22	 * Both pages import this as `../shared/price.js`.
23	 */
24	
25	/**
26	 * A show's cheapest ticket in pounds, or null when the price isn't known.
27	 *
28	 * Reads `priceMin` — the lowest band the show sells, which is what "can I see
29	 * something for under a tenner" actually asks about. Falls back to the `free`
30	 * flag so a catalogue cached before prices shipped (or a free show the price
31	 * pass skipped, having nothing to price) still answers £0 rather than unknown.
32	 *
33	 * @param {object} show a rehydrated catalogue show or an adapted day record
34	 * @returns {number|null} pounds, or null when unknown
35	 */
36	export function showPrice(show) {
37	  if (!show) return null;
38	  if (typeof show.priceMin === "number" && Number.isFinite(show.priceMin)) {
39	    return show.priceMin;
40	  }
41	  return show.free ? 0 : null;
42	}
43	
44	/** The dearest band in pounds, or the cheapest when the show has only one. */
45	export function showPriceMax(show) {
46	  if (!show) return null;
47	  if (typeof show.priceMax === "number" && Number.isFinite(show.priceMax)) {
48	    return show.priceMax;
49	  }
50	  return showPrice(show);
51	}
52	
53	/** Pounds as money: whole amounts lose the ".00" ("£12", not "£12.00"). */
54	export function formatPounds(pounds) {
55	  if (!Number.isFinite(pounds)) return "";
56	  return `£${Number.isInteger(pounds) ? pounds : pounds.toFixed(2)}`;
57	}
58	
59	/**
60	 * What a show costs, as a card would say it: "Free", "£12", "£12–£18", or
61	 * "Price TBC" when we have nothing.
62	 *
63	 * The range is shown only when the show really has more than one band —
64	 * "£12–£12" is noise, and a single-band show is the common case.
65	 *
66	 * @param {object} show
67	 * @returns {string}
68	 */

72	  if (min === 0) return "Free";

104	 */
105	export const PRICE_OPTIONS = [
106	  { value: "any", label: "Any price", short: "Any" },
107	  { value: "free", label: "Free", short: "Free" },

109	];

112	 * Does a show pass a price choice?
113	 *
114	 * @param {object} show
115	 * @param {string} choice one of PRICE_OPTIONS' values ("any" | "free" | "15")
116	 * @returns {boolean} unknown-price shows fail every choice but "any"
117	 */

122	  if (choice === "free") return price === 0;
123	  const cap = Number(choice);

1	// Port of the availability semantics in edfringe/extract.py (UNAVAILABLE_STATUSES,
2	// NON_TICKETED_STATUSES, and the `available` boolean around lines 26-45 & 131-134),
3	// plus small date/time helpers for the shows.json performance shape.
4	//
5	// Field-mapping note (Python model vs. the real shows.json data this runs against):
6	//   - Python's Performance carries `ticket_status` (from the raw event's
7	//     `ticketStatus`); shows.json instead uses the field name `status`. Same
8	//     values, different key — `isAvailable` below reads `perf.status`.
9	//   - Python's Performance has separate `start`/`end` ISO datetimes (end derived
10	//     server-side from `estimatedEndDateTime` or `duration`). shows.json only
11	//     gives `date` + `start` ("HH:MM"), no `end` — see `perfEndMinutes` /
12	//     `perfEndDate`, which derive it from the show's `duration` (minutes),
13	//     falling back to end === start when duration is absent, matching the
14	//     Python fallback of `end = start + timedelta(minutes=dur)` (dur may be None).
15	
16	// A performance is bookable unless its status is one of these (or it's sold
17	// out). Denylist ported verbatim from extract.py's UNAVAILABLE_STATUSES so that
18	// offer statuses like TWO_FOR_ONE / PAY_WHAT_YOU_WANT stay available — they
19	// still sell tickets.
20	export const UNAVAILABLE_STATUSES = new Set([
21	  "SOLD_OUT", "SOLD OUT", "SOLDOUT", "OFF_SALE", "OFFSALE", "NOT_ON_SALE",
22	  "NOT_YET_ON_SALE", "COMING_SOON", "CANCELLED", "CANCELED", "UNAVAILABLE",
23	  "POSTPONED", "SUSPENDED",
24	  // No online allocation left — you'd have to contact the venue, so it can't
25	  // be added to the edfringe basket. Treated as unavailable for scheduling.
26	  "NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE",
27	]);
28	
29	// Statuses where the show is attended for free with no ticket to buy.
30	// Attendable (so available), but the purchase step has nothing to add to the
31	// basket.
32	export const NON_TICKETED_STATUSES = new Set(["FREE_NON_TICKETED"]);
33	
34	/**
35	 * True if a performance is bookable/attendable: not sold out, has a status,
36	 * and that status (uppercased) isn't in the unavailable denylist.
37	 * Mirrors extract.py:
38	 *   available = (not sold_out) and bool(status_norm) and status_norm not in UNAVAILABLE_STATUSES
39	 *
40	 * @param {{soldOut?: boolean, status?: string|null}} perf
41	 * @returns {boolean}
42	 */
43	export function isAvailable(perf) {
44	  if (!perf) return false;
45	  if (perf.soldOut) return false;
46	  const statusNorm = (perf.status || "").trim().toUpperCase();
47	  if (!statusNorm) return false;
48	  return !UNAVAILABLE_STATUSES.has(statusNorm);
49	}
50	
51	/**
52	 * True if a performance's status marks it as free/non-ticketed (attendable,
53	 * but nothing to add to a basket).
54	 * @param {{status?: string|null}} perf
55	 * @returns {boolean}
56	 */
57	export function isNonTicketed(perf) {
58	  const statusNorm = ((perf && perf.status) || "").trim().toUpperCase();
59	  return NON_TICKETED_STATUSES.has(statusNorm);
60	}
61	
62	// --- date/time helpers --------------------------------------------------
63	
64	/**
65	 * Parse a "YYYY-MM-DD" + "HH:MM" pair into minutes since the Unix epoch
66	 * (UTC-based minute count — treats the wall-clock values as-is, with no
67	 * timezone conversion, since shows.json stores local Edinburgh wall-clock
68	 * times and every performance/filter in this app uses the same convention).
69	 * @param {string} date "YYYY-MM-DD"
70	 * @param {string} time "HH:MM"
71	 * @returns {number} minutes since epoch
72	 */
73	export function dateTimeToMinutes(date, time) {
74	  const [y, mo, d] = date.split("-").map(Number);
75	  const [h, mi] = time.split(":").map(Number);
76	  // Date.UTC avoids local-timezone-of-the-running-machine drift; this is a
77	  // pure wall-clock minute count, not a real UTC instant.
78	  return Date.UTC(y, mo - 1, d, h, mi) / 60000;
79	}
80	
81	/**
82	 * Parse a "YYYY-MM-DD" + "HH:MM" pair into a JS Date (UTC-based, wall-clock
83	 * semantics — see dateTimeToMinutes).
84	 * @param {string} date "YYYY-MM-DD"
85	 * @param {string} time "HH:MM"
86	 * @returns {Date}
87	 */
88	export function dateTimeToDate(date, time) {
89	  return new Date(dateTimeToMinutes(date, time) * 60000);
90	}
91	
92	/**
93	 * Minutes-since-midnight for an "HH:MM" string (for time-of-day window
94	 * comparisons independent of date).
95	 * @param {string} time "HH:MM"
96	 * @returns {number}
97	 */
98	export function timeToMinutesOfDay(time) {
99	  const [h, mi] = time.split(":").map(Number);
100	  return h * 60 + mi;
101	}
102	
103	/**
104	 * Compute a performance's end time as minutes-since-epoch, given the show's
105	 * duration in minutes. shows.json has no explicit `end` field (unlike the
106	 * Python model) — this derives it as start + duration, matching the Python
107	 * fallback path where `end` is unset and gets computed from `duration`. When
108	 * durationMins is null/undefined/0, end === start (matches the Python
109	 * behaviour when both estimatedEndDateTime and duration are absent).
110	 * @param {{date: string, start: string}} perf
111	 * @param {number|null|undefined} durationMins
112	 * @returns {number} minutes since epoch
113	 */
114	export function perfEndMinutes(perf, durationMins) {
115	  const startMin = dateTimeToMinutes(perf.date, perf.start);
116	  return durationMins ? startMin + durationMins : startMin;
117	}
118	
119	/**
120	 * Same as perfEndMinutes, but returns a Date.
121	 * @param {{date: string, start: string}} perf
122	 * @param {number|null|undefined} durationMins
123	 * @returns {Date}
124	 */
125	export function perfEndDate(perf, durationMins) {
126	  return new Date(perfEndMinutes(perf, durationMins) * 60000);
127	}

1	/* Geography helpers shared by both front-ends.
2	 *
3	 * This is the first module the Now page (`js/app.js`) and the planner
4	 * (`plan/plan.js`) genuinely share. Both import it as `../shared/geo.js`, which
5	 * resolves to `/shared/geo.js` from either page. Before this existed the values
6	 * below were copy-pasted into both files and nothing tied the copies together —
7	 * a change to one left the pages silently disagreeing.
8	 */
9	
10	/* Very rough bounding box for the UK mainland (lat/lng).
11	 *
12	 * The Now page uses it to ignore a real location that is nowhere near Edinburgh
13	 * (e.g. a tester overseas), keeping the central-Edinburgh default rather than
14	 * moving the pin abroad. The planner uses it to hide its debug menu, which is a
15	 * testing affordance and so only shows when we are not clearly in the UK.
16	 *
17	 * Kept deliberately loose — it only needs to tell "in the UK" from "not". */
18	export const UK_BOUNDS = { minLat: 49.8, maxLat: 59.0, minLng: -8.2, maxLng: 1.9 };
19	
20	/* Is a [lat, lng] roughly within the UK mainland box above? */
21	export function isInUK([lat, lng]) {
22	  return (
23	    lat >= UK_BOUNDS.minLat &&
24	    lat <= UK_BOUNDS.maxLat &&
25	    lng >= UK_BOUNDS.minLng &&
26	    lng <= UK_BOUNDS.maxLng
27	  );
28	}

1	/* Partner (affiliate) links — the site's monetization plumbing.
2	 *
3	 * Pure: no DOM, no fetch. Each front-end renders the returned link itself
4	 * (the planner's schedule-board nags in plan/plan.js), and
5	 * shared/__tests__/affiliates.test.mjs exercises this module directly.
6	 *
7	 * Lives in shared/ rather than plan/ because a partner ID is a property of the
8	 * *site*, not of one page: the planner's "need a place to sleep?" nag and the
9	 * Now page's bookable-place pills both spend the same Booking.com ID, and both
10	 * pages must tag a click the same way or the referral is lost.
11	 *
12	 * Two things a caller needs:
13	 *   1. AFFILIATES — the ID block, empty until the programmes are joined.
14	 *   2. stayLink() / travelLink() — the two links the planner offers, each
15	 *      returning { text, partner, url } so the caller renders "text · partner".
16	 */
17	
18	/* ---------- Monetization: affiliate / referral IDs ----------
19	 *
20	 * These are NOT secrets — they ship in the client, like the analytics token in
21	 * js/analytics.js — and they are empty by default: every link below works as a
22	 * plain deep link, and starts tagging referrals the moment an ID is filled in.
23	 * A partner whose IDs are unset simply stays untagged, so partial set-up is
24	 * fine (join accommodation first, transport later).
25	 *
26	 * TO MONETIZE, join the programmes and paste the IDs here. Which programme, at
27	 * what rate, and the sign-up checklist live in the tracking issue; the short
28	 * version (researched 2026-07-29):
29	 *   - Accommodation → Booking.com. `bookingAid` is the affiliate ID (Booking's
30	 *     own `aid` URL parameter), issued whether you join Booking.com's partner
31	 *     programme direct or through a network (Awin / CJ / Travelpayouts).
32	 *   - Transport → Omio (train + coach + flight in one search, which is what
33	 *     "how do I get to the Fringe?" actually needs). Omio's tracking is issued
34	 *     by whichever network accepts you, so it arrives as a *click wrapper*
35	 *     rather than a query parameter — see CLICK TEMPLATES below.
36	 */
37	export const AFFILIATES = {
38	  // Booking.com's `aid`, plus the `label` we send with it (see stayLink) so the
39	  // dashboard can tell this placement's earnings from any other.
40	  bookingAid: "",
41	  /* CLICK TEMPLATES — a network credits a click by routing it through its own
42	   * domain (awin1.com/cread.php?…&ued=, prf.hn/click/camref:…/destination:,
43	   * tp.media/click?…&deep_link=). The shapes differ per network and the real
44	   * one comes from the dashboard once accepted, so rather than guess a network
45	   * we take its link verbatim with `{deep}` marking where the destination URL
46	   * goes, URL-encoded. Empty template → the plain deep link, untagged. */
47	  bookingClickTemplate: "",
48	  omioClickTemplate: "",
49	};
50	
51	/* Route a destination URL through a network's click wrapper. */
52	function wrapClick(template, url) {
53	  if (!template) return url;
54	  return template.replace("{deep}", encodeURIComponent(url));
55	}
56	
57	/* The day after an ISO date, for the checkout of a stay that ends on the last
58	 * night. Pure calendar maths (UTC noon dodges DST edges), so month and year
59	 * boundaries just work. */
60	export function nextDayISO(dateISO) {
61	  const d = new Date(`${dateISO}T12:00:00Z`);
62	  d.setUTCDate(d.getUTCDate() + 1);
63	  return d.toISOString().slice(0, 10);
64	}
65	
66	/* Somewhere to sleep for the nights of a Fringe trip: a Booking.com search for
67	 * Edinburgh with the trip's own dates pre-filled.
68	 *
69	 * `checkinISO`/`checkoutISO` are the planner's date window. A one-day window
70	 * would ask Booking.com for a zero-night stay (it returns nothing), so a
71	 * checkout that isn't after the check-in becomes the next morning — the honest
72	 * reading of "I'm here on the 12th and need a bed that night".
73	 */
74	export function stayLink({ checkinISO, checkoutISO } = {}, affiliates = AFFILIATES) {
75	  const params = new URLSearchParams({ ss: "Edinburgh" });
76	  if (checkinISO) {
77	    const checkout = checkoutISO && checkoutISO > checkinISO ? checkoutISO : nextDayISO(checkinISO);
78	    params.set("checkin", checkinISO);
79	    params.set("checkout", checkout);
80	  }
81	  if (affiliates.bookingAid) {
82	    params.set("aid", affiliates.bookingAid);
83	    // Booking.com's own per-link tag, so this nag's earnings are attributable.
84	    params.set("label", "edfringenow-plan-night");
85	  }
86	  const url = `https://www.booking.com/searchresults.html?${params}`;
87	  return {
88	    text: "Find a bed",
89	    partner: "Booking.com",
90	    url: wrapClick(affiliates.bookingClickTemplate, url),
91	  };
92	}
93	
94	/* Getting to or out of Edinburgh. Omio's Edinburgh page covers train, coach and
95	 * flight in one search, which is the point: a last-minute Fringe-goer knows
96	 * they need to *get there*, not which mode is cheapest today.
97	 *
98	 * No origin and no date go on the URL. We don't know where the traveller starts
99	 * from (the planner only ever knows Edinburgh), and Omio's route pages key off
100	 * an origin slug, so a guessed one would 404 where the destination page always
101	 * works.
102	 */
103	export function travelLink(affiliates = AFFILIATES) {
104	  const url = "https://www.omio.com/travel/edinburgh";
105	  return {
106	    text: "Trains, coaches & flights",
107	    partner: "Omio",
108	    url: wrapClick(affiliates.omioClickTemplate, url),
109	  };
110	}
111

1	// Cloudflare Web Analytics — privacy-first, cookieless visitor counts.
2	//
3	// Cloudflare Web Analytics sets no cookies, stores no personal data, and can't
4	// track visitors across sites, so it needs no consent banner (see privacy.html).
5	//
6	// The beacon token is NOT a secret — it ships in the client and is visible to
7	// every visitor — so it lives in a GitHub Actions *variable* (not a secret):
8	//   repo Settings -> Secrets and variables -> Actions -> Variables ->
9	//   CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN
10	// The Pages deploy (.github/workflows/pages.yml) injects that value into the
11	// placeholder below at build time, the same way js/build-info.js is stamped.
12	//
13	// TO ENABLE: create a free site in the Cloudflare dashboard (Web Analytics ->
14	// "Add a site"), then add its token as the CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN repo variable.
15	// It works on GitHub Pages as-is — no hosting or DNS move to Cloudflare needed.
16	//
17	// Until a real token is injected (variable unset, or running locally), this
18	// loader does nothing: no beacon is requested, so the site keeps its "no
19	// analytics" behaviour and never ships a broken tag.
20	(function () {
21	  var TOKEN = 'REPLACE_WITH_CLOUDFLARE_WEB_ANALYTICS_TOKEN';
22	  // Bail out while the placeholder is still in place (startsWith, ES5-safe).
23	  if (!TOKEN || TOKEN.lastIndexOf('REPLACE_WITH', 0) === 0) return;
24	
25	  var beacon = document.createElement('script');
26	  beacon.defer = true;
27	  beacon.src = 'https://static.cloudflareinsights.com/beacon.min.js';
28	  beacon.setAttribute('data-cf-beacon', JSON.stringify({ token: TOKEN }));
29	  (document.head || document.documentElement).appendChild(beacon);
30	})();

1	/* Ticket prices, shared by both front-ends.
2	 *
3	 * Until the price scrape landed the site knew only "free" or "paid", because
4	 * that is all the listing API says. Real amounts now come from a separate
5	 * per-performance query, cached once into data/prices.json and folded into the
6	 * data files as `priceMin` / `priceMax` (pounds — see scraper/SCRAPING.md).
7	 *
8	 * Which forces one distinction on every consumer:
9	 *
10	 *   free      the show costs nothing        priceMin === 0
11	 *   priced    we know what it costs         priceMin is a number > 0
12	 *   unknown   we have no price for it       priceMin is null
13	 *
14	 * **Unknown is not free, and it is not "expensive" either.** The price cache is
15	 * fetched once and the festival keeps adding shows, so unknowns are normal and
16	 * permanent, not a bug to design around. A price filter therefore has to say
17	 * what it does with them, and both pages here make the same call: an active
18	 * price cap EXCLUDES unknown-price shows, because a filter must never claim a
19	 * show matches on data it doesn't have. Free is the one bucket that can't be
20	 * wrong — the listing's own flag says so.
21	 *
22	 * Both pages import this as `../shared/price.js`.
23	 */
24	
25	/**
26	 * A show's cheapest ticket in pounds, or null when the price isn't known.
27	 *
28	 * Reads `priceMin` — the lowest band the show sells, which is what "can I see
29	 * something for under a tenner" actually asks about. Falls back to the `free`
30	 * flag so a catalogue cached before prices shipped (or a free show the price
31	 * pass skipped, having nothing to price) still answers £0 rather than unknown.
32	 *
33	 * @param {object} show a rehydrated catalogue show or an adapted day record
34	 * @returns {number|null} pounds, or null when unknown
35	 */
36	export function showPrice(show) {
37	  if (!show) return null;
38	  if (typeof show.priceMin === "number" && Number.isFinite(show.priceMin)) {
39	    return show.priceMin;
40	  }
41	  return show.free ? 0 : null;
42	}
43	
44	/** The dearest band in pounds, or the cheapest when the show has only one. */
45	export function showPriceMax(show) {
46	  if (!show) return null;
47	  if (typeof show.priceMax === "number" && Number.isFinite(show.priceMax)) {
48	    return show.priceMax;
49	  }
50	  return showPrice(show);
51	}
52	
53	/** Pounds as money: whole amounts lose the ".00" ("£12", not "£12.00"). */
54	export function formatPounds(pounds) {
55	  if (!Number.isFinite(pounds)) return "";
56	  return `£${Number.isInteger(pounds) ? pounds : pounds.toFixed(2)}`;
57	}
58	
59	/**
60	 * What a show costs, as a card would say it: "Free", "£12", "£12–£18", or
61	 * "Price TBC" when we have nothing.
62	 *
63	 * The range is shown only when the show really has more than one band —
64	 * "£12–£12" is noise, and a single-band show is the common case.
65	 *
66	 * @param {object} show
67	 * @returns {string}
68	 */
69	export function priceLabel(show) {
70	  const min = showPrice(show);
71	  if (min === null) return "Price TBC";
72	  if (min === 0) return "Free";
73	  const max = showPriceMax(show);
74	  return max > min ? `${formatPounds(min)}–${formatPounds(max)}` : formatPounds(min);
75	}
76	
77	/**
78	 * The price bands the filters offer, cheapest first.
79	 *
80	 * One ladder, used by the Now page's "$" chip and the planner's price facet, so
81	 * the two pages can't drift into offering different money. Each is a *cap*
82	 * ("£15 and under") rather than a slice, because that is the question a
83	 * Fringe-goer with a budget asks — and cumulative caps mean a wider budget can
84	 * only ever add shows, never swap them out.
85	 *
86	 * `free` is its own bucket rather than "≤ £0": free shows are the one group the
87	 * listing flag identifies perfectly, so that option is always trustworthy even
88	 * where the price cache has gaps.
89	 */
90	export const PRICE_CAPS = [10, 15, 20, 30];
91	
92	/**
93	 * The `$` chip / facet options in display order: any, free, then each cap.
94	 *
95	 * Two labels each, because the two places these are rendered have very
96	 * different room. `label` is the unambiguous one ("Up to £15") — used wherever
97	 * it must stand alone: the chip's own value text, aria-labels, the planner's
98	 * facet list. `short` is for the compact segmented control, where six options
99	 * share one narrow dropdown and the surrounding "up to" is said once, by the
100	 * panel's own hint, instead of six times.
101	 *
102	 * "Up to", not "Under": the cap is inclusive, and a £10 ticket turning up under
103	 * "Under £10" is exactly the kind of small lie that loses trust.
104	 */
105	export const PRICE_OPTIONS = [
106	  { value: "any", label: "Any price", short: "Any" },
107	  { value: "free", label: "Free", short: "Free" },
108	  ...PRICE_CAPS.map((c) => ({ value: String(c), label: `Up to £${c}`, short: `£${c}` })),
109	];
110	
111	/**
112	 * Does a show pass a price choice?
113	 *
114	 * @param {object} show
115	 * @param {string} choice one of PRICE_OPTIONS' values ("any" | "free" | "15")
116	 * @returns {boolean} unknown-price shows fail every choice but "any"
117	 */
118	export function matchesPrice(show, choice) {
119	  if (!choice || choice === "any") return true;
120	  const price = showPrice(show);
121	  if (price === null) return false;
122	  if (choice === "free") return price === 0;
123	  const cap = Number(choice);
124	  return Number.isFinite(cap) && price <= cap;
125	}
126

41	  /* CLICK TEMPLATES — a network credits a click by routing it through its own

1	/* Geography helpers shared by both front-ends.
2	 *
3	 * This is the first module the Now page (`js/app.js`) and the planner
4	 * (`plan/plan.js`) genuinely share. Both import it as `../shared/geo.js`, which
5	 * resolves to `/shared/geo.js` from either page. Before this existed the values
6	 * below were copy-pasted into both files and nothing tied the copies together —
7	 * a change to one left the pages silently disagreeing.
8	 */
9	
10	/* Very rough bounding box for the UK mainland (lat/lng).
11	 *
12	 * The Now page uses it to ignore a real location that is nowhere near Edinburgh
13	 * (e.g. a tester overseas), keeping the central-Edinburgh default rather than
14	 * moving the pin abroad. The planner uses it to hide its debug menu, which is a
15	 * testing affordance and so only shows when we are not clearly in the UK.
16	 *
17	 * Kept deliberately loose — it only needs to tell "in the UK" from "not". */
18	export const UK_BOUNDS = { minLat: 49.8, maxLat: 59.0, minLng: -8.2, maxLng: 1.9 };
19	
20	/* Is a [lat, lng] roughly within the UK mainland box above? */
21	export function isInUK([lat, lng]) {
22	  return (
23	    lat >= UK_BOUNDS.minLat &&
24	    lat <= UK_BOUNDS.maxLat &&
25	    lng >= UK_BOUNDS.minLng &&
26	    lng <= UK_BOUNDS.maxLng
27	  );
28	}

- Keyboard: `ArrowUp`/`ArrowDown` on a wheel move one item, smooth-scrolled, clamped (`app.js:1940-1946`).
- Wheel scroll mask: `mask-image: linear-gradient(to bottom, transparent, #000 32%, #000 68%, transparent)` (`styles.css:1081-1082`).

### 3.4 Count + pick list states (`renderConstraintShows`, `app.js:2152-2211`)
Candidate pool `constraintShows()` = all loaded shows with `timeToMinutes(s.time) >= NOW.minutes`. **Deliberately ignores the genre/subgenre/price filters** (`app.js:436-438`).

| Condition | `#constraintCount` | `#constraintCountLab` | `#showPickList` |
|---|---|---|---|
| No future start times at all | `0` | `shows later today` | `<p class="picklist-empty">No later shows to aim for today.</p>` |
| Times exist, none at the chosen minute | count of shows at chosen time (0) | `shows start at HH:MM` | `<p class="picklist-empty">No shows start exactly then. Nearest:</p>` + `.timepick-suggest` with up to **4** buttons |
| ≥1 show at the chosen time | animated count | `show starts at HH:MM` (n=1) / `shows start at HH:MM` | one `.show-pick` button per show |

- Nearest-time suggestion buttons read `` `${clockLabel(t)} · ${count}` `` e.g. `18:30 · 7` (`app.js:2181-2184`). Click → `setConstraintTime(t)` + `syncWheels(true)`.
- `.show-pick` button markup (`app.js:2199-2209`): `.sp-radio` (custom radio; selected state `.is-sel` draws a gold dot, `styles.css:1114`), `.sp-title` = show title, `.sp-venue` = venue, `.sp-genre` = genre, and — **only when `showPrice(s) !== null`** — ` · ` + `priceLabel(s)`. Then `subgenreTags(s)`. Staggered `animation-delay: ${i*40}ms` with `.anim` class when animating.
- Count animation `tweenCount` (`app.js:2214-2233`): cubic ease-out over **380 ms**, plus a `.bump` class. Skipped entirely under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` (also `styles.css:1377-1379`).

### 3.5 Interactions in the panel
- **Tap a `.show-pick`** → `selectConstraintShow(id)` (`app.js:2136-2148`): sets it as the commitment, clears any place/note, clears `legShowId` if it was that show, resets `spareCtaDismissed=false`, resets list page cap, then `refreshMap()` and **closes all panels**.
- **Roll a wheel** → `setConstraintTime(hhmm)` (`app.js:2117-2131`): browses only. Clears `selectedShowId`, `destLabel`, `destPlace`, `destNote`, resets `spareCtaDismissed`, list cap; re-renders.
- **Type in `#destInput`** (`app.js:1958-1971`): mirrors into `state.destLabel`, enables/disables `#destFind` on non-empty trimmed value, and **invalidates** any previously found place or note.
- **Enter in `#destInput`** with non-empty value → `findPlaceOnMap()` (`app.js:1972-1977`).
- **Click `#destFind`** → `findPlaceOnMap()`.

### 3.6 Place search (geocoding) — `findPlaceOnMap`, `app.js:2000-2031`
- One search at a time (`placeSearchInFlight`).
- While in flight the button is disabled and its text becomes **`Finding…`**; restored to the previous label afterwards.
- URL: `https://nominatim.openstreetmap.org/search?` with `q`, `format=jsonv2`, `limit=5`, `addressdetails=1`, `viewbox=${minLng},${maxLat},${maxLng},${minLat}` (`places.js:66-77`). **Not** `bounded=1` — see the comment at `places.js:17-26`.
- Edinburgh box: `{ minLat: 55.87, maxLat: 56.0, minLng: -3.46, maxLng: -3.02 }` (`places.js:27`). Out-of-box hits are dropped client-side (`places.js:155`).
- Exactly one result → committed immediately (`commitPlace`), no result list.
- Otherwise → `renderPlaceResults(q, places)`.

**Result-box copy** (`app.js:2039-2069`) in `#destResults`:
| State | `.place-msg` text |
|---|---|
| Search threw / non-OK HTTP (`places === null`) | `Map search isn’t reachable right now.` |
| ≥1 hit | `Which one?` |
| 0 hits | `Couldn’t find “<q>” around Edinburgh.` (curly quotes) |

Each hit is a `<button class="place-hit" data-i="i">` with `.ph-ico` = `placeIcon(kind)`, `.ph-title` = label, and `.ph-area` = street/neighbourhood/suburb when present. A trailing row is **always** appended: `<button class="place-hit place-hit--note">` with `📝` and title `Keep “<q>” as a note`.

**Place kinds and icons** (`places.js:83-134`): `restaurant 🍽️`, `cafe ☕`, `pub 🍺`, `train 🚆`, `hotel 🛏️`, `attraction 🏛️`, `theatre 🎭`, `other 📍`. Bucketing rules: `railway` + `station|halt|stop` → train; `building`+`train_station` → train; `amenity` restaurant/food_court/biergarten → restaurant; cafe/fast_food/ice_cream → cafe; pub/bar/nightclub → pub; theatre/arts_centre → theatre; camera_obscura/planetarium → attraction; `tourism` hotel/hostel/guest_house/apartment → hotel; museum/attraction/gallery/viewpoint/zoo/theme_park → attraction; `historic` → attraction; else `other`.
**De-duplication**: same label within `NEARBY_LAT 0.004` / `NEARBY_LNG 0.006` is one place; a typed duplicate replaces a kept `other` (`places.js:141, 165-176`).

- `commitPlace` (`app.js:2083-2098`): pins it, clears `selectedShowId`, resets both dismiss flags, fills the input with the label, clears results, refreshes and closes panels.
- `commitPlaceNote` (`app.js:2103-2113`): label-only, **also clears `legShowId`** (no coordinates ⇒ can't judge fit), no pin, no route.

- `friendlyDuration` bands (`shared/duration.js:44-65`): `< 60` → `"45 minutes"`; `60–120` → `"1 hour and 20 minutes"` (exactly 60/120 → `"1 hour"` / `"2 hours"`); `> 120` → `"about 2½ hours"` (rounded to nearest half hour). Negative/non-finite → `""`.

**4.7 Destination node** (`destNode`, `app.js:1363-1367`): icon = genre icon for a show or `placeIcon(kind)` for a place; time `clockLabel(constraint.time)`; title = `destinationLabel()`; sub = **`Your next commitment`**; extra = partner link for a place.

**4.8 Node controls** (`wireNodeControls`, `app.js:1194-1211`) added to `.plan-node.stop` and `.plan-node.dest`; node gets class `has-node-controls`:

- Stop: `aria-label="Pick a different show"` / `"Remove selected show"`. Change → smooth-scrolls `#shows` into view (`block: "start"`); Remove → clears `legShowId` and refreshes.
- Dest: `aria-label="Change your next commitment"` / `"Remove your next commitment"`. Change → `openConstraintEditor()` (reopens `#constraintPanel`, sets `editingCommitment`, smooth-scrolls it to `block: "center"`, `app.js:640-649`); Remove → `clearCommitment()` (`app.js:654-667`) which clears time/show/label/place/note and both dismiss flags but **keeps** the selected show.

**4.9 Spare-time prompt** (`spareCtaNode`, `app.js:1307-1320`) — occupies the plan's middle slot when a commitment exists and no show is slipped in.
- Rendered only when: not dismissed, `planSpareMinutes()` is non-null and `> 0`, and `fittingShows().length > 0`. Otherwise the slot falls back to a plain `planLeg`.

- `planSpareMinutes()` (`app.js:1277-1298`): with a fitting leg, arrival = leg start + leg duration + travel(leg→dest); otherwise arrival = `NOW.minutes` + travel(you→dest). Spare = `round(constraint start − arrival)`.
